stories.title: Model context protocol eliminates session state for horizontal scaling
stories.social_post:
The Model Context Protocol has abandoned stateful session handshakes in favor of stateless, horizontally scalable servers. This architectural pivot removes protocol-level sessions, allowing server instances behind load balancers to handle requests without pinning client connections to specific nodes.

Handling multi-turn interactions across stateless infrastructure required introducing Multi Round-Trip Requests. Rather than letting servers initiate out-of-band requests back to clients, the protocol now structures elicitation flows as explicit round trips that preserve state on the client side. This shift also makes tool discovery and capability negotiation fully cacheable.

Agentic systems cannot scale reliably when individual tool servers hold volatile memory. Pushing session coordination outward into client contexts aligns tool orchestration with standard distributed systems architecture, where ephemeral server processes can crash or restart without breaking long-running reasoning loops.

Treating tools as stateless HTTP-native endpoints makes agent infrastructure vastly easier to deploy and maintain.
stories.why_read: Read this to understand how the Model Context Protocol is moving toward stateless architecture and HTTP-native primitives. You will learn how eliminating session handshakes enables horizontal scaling and improves agentic messaging.

stories.title: Why formal verification makes Lean faster than Rust
stories.social_post:
Pairing autonomous AI coders with formal verification unlocks radical performance gains that traditional testing cannot safely permit.

A benchmark on the 212 megabyte Silesia corpus reveals that a DEFLATE implementation written in Lean completed compression in 4.57 seconds, decisively beating the 5.77 seconds of miniz_oxide, the standard pure-Rust library, while matching or exceeding its compression ratio.

The underlying mechanism relies on a machine-checked proof theorem that guarantees round-trip decompression correctness. Because the compiler mathematically verifies that any change preserves exact behavior, engineers can instruct autonomous agents to apply aggressive, non-trivial algorithmic rewrites without fear of subtle regression or silent data corruption.

Most teams restrict generative coding tools because manual code review cannot keep up with complex optimizations. Formal verification flips this dynamic by providing an automated, mathematical guardrail that turns autonomous code generation from a liability into a high-throughput performance engine.

Formal proofs are no longer just an academic curiosity; they are the ultimate safety harness for autonomous AI engineering.
stories.why_read: Read this to understand how machine-checked formal proofs allow AI agents to aggressively optimize code without risking correctness. It illustrates a compelling mechanism by which verified functional programming can outperform standard systems languages.

stories.title: Analyzing workload evolution and traffic in production llm serving
stories.social_post:
Production LLM traffic behaves fundamentally differently from the synthetic benchmarks engineering teams rely on to size their clusters. A longitudinal study of a one-year production serving trace shows that aggregate request rates hide severe skew across user sessions and individual model architectures.

KV cache hit rates degrade significantly under multi-tenant conditions unless routing layers actively preserve session affinity to specific worker nodes. Standard round-robin and least-connections load balancers destroy prefix caching locality, forcing redundant attention recomputation across GPU workers. The trace data reveals that long-tail models experience bursty, unpredictable cold starts that choke serving pipelines when memory capacity is static.

Dynamic cache partitioning and prompt-aware request dispatching deliver massive throughput gains compared to conventional server scheduling. System architects designing inference gateways cannot treat language models as generic stateless microservices.

Understanding actual production access patterns is essential to avoid over-provisioning expensive accelerator memory.
stories.why_read: Read this to understand how real-world LLM serving workloads evolve over an entire year across diverse models and users. You will learn key empirical insights on caching and load balancing derived from an open production trace.
